output.brief: The evidence points mainly to the scholarship cut, not the Admissions Office. Applications and admits rose, so the applicant pool wasn't the problem. Yield fell only in the tiers whose awards were cut: Dean's from $14,000 to $9,000 and Merit from $9,000 to $5,000. Yield barely moved for Presidential awards (unchanged) or for students with no merit award. Early-action yield also fell about as much as regular-decision yield (45.2% to 37.8%, against 39.0% to 31.5%), even though early-action decisions went out on time on the old system. So slow portal turnaround can't be the main driver, though it was real and probably cost some individual students. I'm fairly confident, but we haven't separated early action from regular decision within each tier, and the missing-transcript complaints are unresolved. Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take the award schedule back to the finance committee with the revenue trade-off modelled, targeting the tiers whose yield fell, before award letters go out. Also set a regular-decision turnaround target and check the missing-transcript reports. Hold the vendor rebuild until that check shows a real fault.
